## (Computer Exercise) Retrieve the daily stock prices of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) over the period of 2016–2019 from Yahoo! Finance using the quantmod package. Compute the daily log returns from closing prices as differences of log prices.

```{r message = FALSE}
library("quantmod")
library(forecast)
library(tseries)
library(ggplot2)
library(FinTS)
library(rugarch)
```

```{r}
getSymbols("JPM", from="2016-01-01", to="2019-12-31",src="yahoo", auto.assign=TRUE)
```

## (a) Plot the return and squared return time series. Do you observe volatility clustering? 
```{r}
P <- JPM$JPM.Close
R <- diff(log(P))[-1]
plot(R)
```
```{r}
plot(R^2)
```

In both plots we observe volatility clustering. 

## (b) Do you find serial correlations and ARCH effects in the returns according to the ACF, PACF, and portmanteau tests? Explain.

```{r}
tsdisplay(R)
```
```{r}
Box.test(R, lag = 10, type="Ljung-Box")
```

From the ACF, PCF, Ljung-Box we can see that return time series is not showing serially correlations.
```{r}
tsdisplay(R^2)
```


```{r}
Box.test(R^2, lag = 10, type="Ljung-Box") 
```
```{r}
ArchTest(R, 10)
```
From the ACF, PCF, Ljung-Box test we can see that squared return time series is showing highly serially auto correlations which is evidence of Arch effect and from Lagrange multiplier test we can see there is an Arch effect.


## (c) Fit a Gaussian ARMA(0,0)-GARCH(1,1) model to the return series. Perform model checking. In particular, check the normal QQ-plot of the standardized residuals. Explain whether the model is adequate.

```{r}
spec_garch11 <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(garchOrder=c(1,1)), 
                          mean.model = list(armaOrder=c(0,0)))
fit_garch11 <- ugarchfit(spec=spec_garch11, data=R)
fit_garch11
```

From the statistics we can see that there is no serially correlations in standardized residuals and standardized squared residuals. Also ARCH LM test is showing that there is no ARCH effect. All coefficients are significant. So the model is adequate. 

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(3,2));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
plot(fit_garch11,which=1)
plot(fit_garch11,which=3)
plot(fit_garch11,which=10)
plot(fit_garch11,which=11)
plot(fit_garch11,which=8)
plot(fit_garch11,which=9)
```
However, QQ plot is showing that our error is not normally distributed and we observe a fat tail. 


## (d) Fit an ARMA(0,0)-GARCH(1,1) model with standardized Student-t innovations to the returns. Perform model checking, including showing the QQ-plot and the series with 2 conditional standard deviations superimposed. Explain whether the model is adequate. Write down the fitted model.
```{r}
spec_garch11std <- ugarchspec(variance.model = list(garchOrder=c(1,1)), 
                           mean.model = list(armaOrder=c(0,0)),
                           distribution.model = "std")
fit_garch11std <- ugarchfit(spec=spec_garch11std, data=R)
fit_garch11std
```


```{r}
par(mfrow=c(3,2));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
plot(fit_garch11std,which=1)
plot(fit_garch11std,which=3)
plot(fit_garch11std,which=10)
plot(fit_garch11std,which=11)
plot(fit_garch11std,which=8)
plot(fit_garch11std,which=9)
```
We can observe that the shape variable is very significant and also QQ plot is showing that the residual is following t student distribution.


$$r_t - 0.000650 = \epsilon_{t}, \epsilon_{t} = \sqrt{h_{t}} v_{t}, \quad v_{t} \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}t_{df = 3.700767}, h_{t} = 0.000019 + 0.145256 \epsilon_{t-1}^2 + 0.765638 h_{t-1}.$$


## (e) Compute the 1- to 10-step ahead forecasts of the returns and conditional standard deviation based on the model you obtained in part (d).

```{r}
(fcst_garch11std <- ugarchforecast(fit_garch11std, n.ahead=10))
```
```{r}
par(mfrow=c(2,1));par(mar=c(3,3,3,3))
plot(fcst_garch11std, which=1)
plot(fcst_garch11std, which=3)
```
